title: Tenant Service Discovery and Connection Contract for Private Deployments
author: Aisha Navarro
content:
Overview:

This document defines the service discovery and connection contract that Redwood operators and customers must follow for Private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It establishes the canonical DNS patterns, connection semantics, security expectations (TLS/mTLS, ephemeral credentials, KMS boundaries), operational SLOs for connectivity, and automated acceptance tests used during onboarding and upgrades. The contract is intentionally prescriptive to ensure cross-team compatibility (runtime, control-plane, operator) and to make day‑2 operations deterministic.

Scope:
- Applies to all Private deployment modes: VPC-hosted customers, dedicated on-prem appliances, and hybrid edge bridges managed by Redwood.
- Covers control-plane endpoints, model-serving frontends, telemetry collectors, KV-cache replication endpoints, and operator-admin interfaces.
- Does not cover customer internal-only services that are outside Redwood’s ingress/egress surface.

Definitions:
- tenant-runtime: the per-tenant serving process (GPU-backed) that accepts API requests.
- control-proxy: the control plane’s egress/ingress proxy used for model management and metrics.
- mgmt-endpoint: operator-facing administrative endpoints (bastion/SSH, agent control).
- service-fqdn: the fully-qualified domain name assigned to a Redwood service for a tenant.

Design principles:
1) Explicit naming: every tenant-visible endpoint uses a stable service-fqdn. Names are immutable during a major release to avoid TTL/rotation issues.
2) Small, well-defined port surface: minimize open ports to reduce attack surface and simplify firewall rules.
3) Defense-in-depth: TLS mandatory, mTLS for operator/control channels, and ephemeral credentials for tenant APIs.
4) Observable health: every service must expose a /healthz and a header-aware readiness endpoint.

Service FQDN and Port Matrix (required):
| Logical service name | FQDN pattern (customer-visible) | Port | Protocol | SLO (connectivity) | Notes |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------- | ---- | -------- | ------------------ | ----- |
| tenant-api | tenant.<customer>.private.redwood.net | 443 | HTTPS (HTTP/2 allowed) | 99.95% p95 connect within 150ms | TLS1.3 required, ALPN h2 or http/1.1 |
| control-proxy | control.<customer>.private.redwood.net | 8443 | mTLS (HTTP/2 preferred) | 99.99% p99 connect within 100ms | Client certs rotated monthly |
| kv-replica | kv.<customer>.private.redwood.net | 7000 | TLS-wrapped TCP | 99.9% p95 connect within 200ms | One-way allowlist + port ACLs |
| telemetry-ingest | telem-<customer>.collector.internal | 6514 | TLS (syslog/HTTPS) | 99.9% p95 connect within 250ms | Support sampling and backpressure headers |
| operator-mgmt | mgmt-admin.<region>.redwoodops.internal | 22/8444 | SSH / HTTPS | 99.99% availability for operators | Access limited by operator VPN and RBAC |

DNS and TTL rules:
- Registered names must be CNAMEs to regional endpoints when possible to allow safe operator failover.
- Default TTL: 60s for production tenant endpoints. Lower TTLs (30s) require explicit operator approval.
- When rotating endpoints during deploy/upgrade, maintain old IPs for at least 2x max DNS TTL + 60s to ensure outstanding connections drain gracefully.

Firewall and Network ACL expectations (customer + operator):
1) Customer must permit outbound connections to required service FQDNs and ports listed above.
2) Operator-provided peering or Transit must implement least-privilege ACLs: allow only listed source CIDRs and ports.
3) For on-prem air-gapped sites using edge bridge, a one-way egress tunnel over TLS to telemetry-ingest is required; inbound connections are proxied via control-proxy.

Connection semantics and timeouts:
- Idle connection timeout (load-balancer): 300s for tenant-api; 60s for control-proxy.
- Backend keepalive: runtime must support HTTP keepalive and connection reuse for serialized requests. Documented keepalive: 90s.
- Client should implement exponential backoff with jitter for connection failures: base 200ms, cap 30s, max retries 3 for idempotent calls.
- Health check expectations: 2 consecutive successful probes to mark healthy; 3 failed probes to mark unhealthy. Probe interval: 10s, timeout: 3s.

Security and cryptography:
- TLS minimum: TLS 1.3. Weak ciphers disabled.
- mTLS required for control-proxy and operator-mgmt channels. Client certificates are issued by Redwood CA and rotated monthly.
- Tenant API authentication: short-lived bearer tokens (recommended JWT with 15m lifetime) or ephemeral API keys issued by the control plane. Long-lived keys require explicit approval and key-scoped ACLs.
- KMS boundary: all tenant secrets used to authenticate with model artifacts and S3-like stores must be secured by customer-managed KMS in Private deployments where requested. Provide KMS attestation URL in onboarding metadata.
- HSM/KMS integration: for regulated customers requiring HSM, use dedicated KMS endpoints and the HSM workflow in the operator handoff checklist.

Acceptance test suite (automated) — executed during onboarding and every major upgrade:
1) DNS resolution test: resolve service-fqdn to at least one IP within 100ms from each configured customer region.
2) TLS handshake test: establish TLS1.3 handshake and verify CA chain and certificate CN matches expected pattern.
3) mTLS test: for control-proxy, present operator client cert and validate mutual handshake.
4) Throughput smoke: send 100 concurrent small requests to tenant-api, verify 95% success within p95 latency threshold.
5) KV replication spot-check: write/read pair to kv-replica and validate consistency at T+5s.
6) Telemetry ingestion: send 1k events; assert no more than 0.5% lost and that ingest latency p95 < 1s for sampled events.

Operator onboarding checklist (field copy for customer handoff):
- Pre-installation:
  1) Confirm CIDR lists and peering details with customer (attach signed connectivity matrix).
  2) Validate KMS/HSM endpoints and token-scope policies.
  3) Exchange root-of-trust thumbprints for CA (operator and customer).
- Install/commission:
  1) Provision CNAMEs and validate DNS TTL.
  2) Install operator client certs and verify mTLS channel with control-proxy.
  3) Run acceptance test suite and resolve any failures before cutover.
- Post-cutover verification:
  1) Monitor p95 connect latency and dropped-connections for 1h.
  2) Verify telemetry sampling and cost-attribution headers are present.
  3) Record evidence bundle (acceptance logs, DNS snapshot, cert chain) and attach to customer record.

Upgrade and rollback implications for the contract:
- Backwards compatibility: ensure new runtime or control-plane versions are compatible with existing service-fqdn and TLS expectations. Breaking changes to port/protocol require 60-day customer notice and a staged migration.
- Rolling upgrade pattern: use CNAME shadowing and traffic-shifting so that a subset of tenants point to the new endpoint. Validate acceptance tests on shadowed tenants before broad roll.
- Emergency rollback: operator must restore previous CNAME targets and reintroduce previous certificates into the trust store. Verify certificate validity and health checks before marking rollback complete.

Operational SLOs and alerting thresholds (connectivity-focused):
- Tenant API connectivity: availability 99.95% monthly; alert when per-tenant p95 connect latency exceeds 200ms for >5 minutes.
- Control-proxy connectability: 99.99% monthly; page on p99 failures > 1 minute.
- KV replication: replication lag < 500ms p95; page on sustained lag > 2s for > 10 minutes.

Troubleshooting playbook (quick steps):
1) DNS: confirm A/CNAME records and TTL; use dig +trace and validate from customer region.
2) TLS: openssl s_client -connect <host>:443 -servername <host> -alpn h2 to check handshake details.
3) mTLS: check cert chain and OCSP stapling; if cert mismatch, pull operator CA thumbprint from stored evidence.
4) Network path: run traceroute, check peering ACLs and Transit logs for blocked ports.
5) Observe agent logs in operator-mgmt and control-proxy for TLS alerting (e.g., SNI mismatch).

Sample terraform snippet (customer outbound security group):
```hcl
resource "aws_security_group_rule" "allow_redwood_tenant_api" {
  type              = "egress"
  from_port         = 443
  to_port           = 443
  protocol          = "tcp"
  cidr_blocks       = ["10.0.0.0/8"]
  description       = "Allow outbound HTTPS to tenant API (replace with Redwood FQDN IPs)"
}
```

Sample client connection YAML (runtime SDK configuration):
```yaml
runtime:
  endpoint: "https://tenant.acme.private.redwood.net"
  tls:
    min_version: "TLS1.3"
    alpn: ["h2","http/1.1"]
  auth:
    method: "ephemeral"
    token_ttl: 900
  timeouts:
    connect_ms: 150
    read_ms: 30000
```

Evidence and audit requirements:
- Store acceptance test results, DNS snapshots, cert chains, and signed connectivity matrices for a minimum of 2 years for regulated customers.
- For customers using customer-managed KMS, include KMS attestation URL in the evidence bundle.

Appendix — Common failure modes and mitigations:
- Symptom: TLS handshake fails for some clients. Possible causes: SNI mismatch, missing ALPN, incomplete CA chain. Mitigation: validate cert CN/SAN, check ALPN values, reissue certs with proper SANs.
- Symptom: Intermittent DNS resolution failures. Possible causes: TTL too low, recursive resolver caching misconfiguration. Mitigation: increase TTL to 60s, add secondary authoritative nameserver, monitor resolver error rates.
- Symptom: KV replication lag on failover. Possible causes: network partition, CPU saturation on replicas. Mitigation: promote healthy replica, throttle warm writes, schedule replication catch-up window.
